    Content from The question and the data

    Last updated on 2026-10-30 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • What causal question does the 401(k) example ask?
    • Why can we not answer it by comparing eligible and non-eligible households?

    Objectives

    • Name the treatment, the outcome and the confounders in the 401(k) example
    • Load the data and compute the raw gap in net financial assets
    • Show that eligibility and savings both rise with income
    • Use a causal diagram to decide which variables belong in the adjustment set
    Callout

    From the masterclass

    If you came to the masterclass, welcome back. This lesson picks up where Part 4 of the masterclass slides left off, and we will work through the same example in more depth. In this episode we go back over:

    • slide 8, “A confounder affects both the treatment and the outcome”;
    • slide 10, “Two possible outcomes per household, and we only see one”, and the Part 1 summary on slide 11;
    • slide 21, “Which variables should we adjust for?”;
    • slide 29, “Our example: does a workplace pension increase household savings?”.

    All the code in this lesson follows DoubleML’s own example, Impact of 401(k) on Financial Wealth, which is available in both Python and R. Where code appears on a slide, you will find it here unchanged.

    The question

    A 401(k) is a workplace pension in the United States. Employers do not have to offer one, and in 1991, when these data were collected, some did and some did not. The example asks:

    Did being eligible for a 401(k) raise a household’s net financial assets?

    In other words, if two households were alike in every way that matters except that one was eligible and the other was not, how much more would the eligible household hold?

    Callout

    What is a 401(k), if you are not from the US?

    A 401(k) is a retirement savings account offered through work, and it takes its name from the section of the US tax code that created it. Workers choose how much of their pay to put in, usually before tax, and many employers add a matching amount. As with Australian superannuation or a UK workplace pension, the money builds up in the worker’s own account.

    The difference for our purposes is that a 401(k) is optional. US employers choose whether to offer one, and in 1991, the year of our data, workers chose whether to join. Australian employers, by contrast, must pay at least 12% of wages into super, and UK employers have had to enrol eligible workers automatically since this was phased in from 2012, although workers can opt out. In this example, “eligible” means that the household’s employer offered a 401(k) (slide 29).

    We will use the notation from the slides:

    • The treatment D is eligibility (e401), which is 1 if the household is eligible and 0 if it is not.
    • The outcome Y is net financial assets in US dollars (net_tfa). This adds up bank accounts, savings bonds, stocks, and IRA and 401(k) balances, and subtracts non-mortgage debt.
    • The confounders X are the things that affect both eligibility and savings. Here they are income, age, education, family size, marital status, whether there are two earners, whether someone has another (defined benefit) pension, IRA participation and home ownership.

    The data

    The data cover 9,915 households from the 1991 Survey of Income and Program Participation, the same sample that Chernozhukov et al. (2018) used. Let’s start with step 1 from the slides (slide 35):

    PYTHON 

    !pip install doubleml     # once per session
import numpy as np
import doubleml as dml
from doubleml.datasets import fetch_401K

data = fetch_401K(return_type='DataFrame')
print(data[['e401', 'net_tfa']]
      .groupby('e401').mean().diff())

    OUTPUT 

              net_tfa
e401
0             NaN
1     19559.34475

    The first line installs DoubleML. In Jupyter or Colab, a line that starts with ! runs as a command outside Python. If you followed the Setup page, DoubleML is already installed and pip will simply tell you so. fetch_401K downloads the data, so you will need an internet connection.

    The last two lines compute the raw gap, which is the average net financial assets of eligible households minus the average for households that were not eligible. In the output, diff() puts that difference in the row for 1, and you should see that eligible households held about $19,559 more.

    Let’s look at the variables we will use:

    PYTHON 

    print(data.shape)
data[['net_tfa', 'e401', 'p401', 'inc', 'age', 'educ', 'fsize']].describe().round(1)

    OUTPUT 

    (9915, 14)
         net_tfa    e401    p401       inc     age    educ   fsize
count     9915.0  9915.0  9915.0    9915.0  9915.0  9915.0  9915.0
mean     18051.5     0.4     0.3   37200.6    41.1    13.2     2.9
std      63522.5     0.5     0.4   24774.3    10.3     2.8     1.5
min    -502302.0     0.0     0.0   -2652.0    25.0     1.0     1.0
25%       -500.0     0.0     0.0   19413.0    32.0    12.0     2.0
50%       1499.0     0.0     0.0   31476.0    40.0    12.0     3.0
75%      16524.5     1.0     1.0   48583.5    48.0    16.0     4.0
max    1536798.0     1.0     1.0  242124.0    64.0    18.0    13.0

    The variable p401 records whether the household actually took part in a 401(k). Only eligible households can take part, so p401 is 1 for a subset of the eligible ones.

    Plotting the data

    The DoubleML example uses seaborn for its plots, so we set that up first:

    PYTHON 

    import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

sns.set()
colors = sns.color_palette()

    How many households were eligible, and how many of them took part? We can plot eligibility first:

    PYTHON 

    data['e401'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar', color=colors)
plt.title('Eligibility, 401(k)')
plt.xlabel('e401')
_ = plt.ylabel('count')
plt.show()

    Then we make the same plot for participation:

    PYTHON 

    data['p401'].value_counts().plot(kind='bar', color=colors)
plt.title('Participation, 401(k)')
plt.xlabel('p401')
_ = plt.ylabel('count')
plt.show()

    You should see that 2,594 of the 3,682 eligible households took part. Next we plot the outcome, separately for households that were and were not eligible:

    PYTHON 

    _ = sns.displot(data, x="net_tfa", hue="e401", col="e401",
                kind="kde", fill=True)
plt.show()

    Each curve shows how net financial assets are spread across households, and a curve is highest where households are most common. In both groups most households hold little and a few hold a great deal, but the curve for eligible households stretches further to the right.

    The DoubleML example also computes the raw gap for taking part:

    PYTHON 

    print(data[['p401', 'net_tfa']].groupby('p401').mean().diff())

    OUTPUT 

               net_tfa
p401
0              NaN
1     27371.582031

    Households that took part held about $27,372 more than those that did not.

    Why does the raw gap mislead?

    Eligibility came with the job, and better-paid jobs offered a 401(k) more often. Income also affects how much a household can save, whether or not it has a pension. This makes income a confounder (slide 8), because it pushes eligibility and savings up together. We can see this by splitting households into five income bands:

    PYTHON 

    bands = pd.qcut(data['inc'], 5, labels=['lowest', '2', '3', '4', 'highest'])
data.groupby(bands, observed=True)[['e401', 'net_tfa']].mean().astype(float).round(2)

    OUTPUT 

             e401   net_tfa
inc
lowest   0.13   1565.61
2        0.26   4713.01
3        0.38   9801.01
4        0.49  19138.48
highest  0.59  55039.57

    Each row is a fifth of the households, ordered from the lowest incomes to the highest. The e401 column gives the share that were eligible and net_tfa gives their average net financial assets. You should see both columns rise as income rises.

    So the raw gap mixes the effect of eligibility with the fact that eligible households earn more and would have saved more anyway. The Part 1 summary on slide 11 put this into words by saying that a raw comparison mixes the effect with selection bias. Using the potential outcomes from slide 10, we can write it as

    \[\underbrace{E[Y \mid D=1] - E[Y \mid D=0]}_{\text{raw gap}} = \underbrace{E[Y(1) - Y(0) \mid D=1]}_{\text{effect on the eligible}} + \underbrace{E[Y(0) \mid D=1] - E[Y(0) \mid D=0]}_{\text{selection bias}},\]

    where Y(1) is what a household would hold if eligible and Y(0) is what the same household would hold if not. Every household has both, but we only ever see one of them. E[ ] means “the average of”. The selection bias term is the difference between the two groups that has nothing to do with the pension, and in this example it is almost certainly positive.

    Which variables should we adjust for?

    The argument behind the example comes from Poterba et al. (1995). Around 1991, they argue, people chose jobs for the pay and the work rather than for the 401(k), so once income and a few other characteristics are held fixed, eligibility is close to as good as random. This is a claim about the causal diagram below, and we have no way to prove it from the data.

    In a causal diagram, an arrow means “causes”. The nine confounders in X point to both eligibility and assets, so they open a back-door path (eligibility ← X → assets), and we close that path by adjusting for X. The dashed box is a confounder that nobody measured.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: should participation go in X?

    The data include p401 (taking part). Should it be one of the confounders?

    No. Eligibility causes taking part, since only eligible households can take part, and taking part changes savings. That puts p401 on the path from the treatment to the outcome, which makes it a mediator. If we adjusted for it, we would remove the part of the effect that works through taking part, and that is most of it. A mediator is one kind of bad control (Cinelli et al., 2024). Another kind is a collider, something caused by both the treatment and the outcome (slide 21). Adjusting for a collider creates a link between them that is not really there.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: what is missing?

    Think of one thing that could affect both eligibility and savings but does not appear in the data.

    The DoubleML example names one, a preference for saving. People who like to save may have looked for jobs that offered a pension, and they would hold more assets anyway. No variable in the survey measures this preference, so no method that adjusts for X can remove it. In episode 5 we will ask how strong a confounder like this would need to be to change the answer.

    Key Points
    • The treatment is 401(k) eligibility (e401), the outcome is net financial assets (net_tfa), and the nine confounders include income, age and education.
    • Eligible households held $19,559 more on average, but eligibility and savings both rise with income, so this raw gap mixes the effect with selection bias.
    • A causal diagram tells us what goes in X: confounders go in, and mediators such as taking part (p401) stay out.
    • Adjusting for X cannot remove a confounder that was never measured, such as a preference for saving.

    Content from How DML works, by hand

    Last updated on 2026-10-30 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do two predictions and one regression cut a confounder out of the comparison?
    • What does a residual mean for one household?
    • Why does each household’s prediction come from a model that never saw it?

    Objectives

    • Predict savings and eligibility from the confounders with random forests, using cross-fitting
    • Compute the residuals and estimate the effect as the slope of one on the other
    • Check that with straight-line predictions the same steps give the ordinary regression coefficient
    • Show what goes wrong when a flexible model predicts the households it was trained on
    Callout

    From the masterclass

    In this episode we build by hand what the slides showed in pictures:

    • slide 30, “How DML cuts the confounder out” (model 1 predicts savings, model 2 predicts eligibility, and each keeps only the residual, actual minus predicted);
    • slide 31, the same four steps with smoking, exercise and heart disease;
    • slide 32, one household’s residuals, the final regression \(Y - \hat{Y} = \theta(D - \hat{D}) + \varepsilon\), and its slope across all households;
    • slide 33, “Cross-fitting: models never predict households they trained on”.

    A residual is actual minus predicted: what is left over once the prediction is taken away. That is why the chart on slide 32 and slide 33 call them “leftovers”. It is the same thing, and in this lesson we say residual.

    In episode 3 DoubleML will do all of this in a few lines, so working through it once by hand here should make it easier to see what those lines are doing.

    Set up

    If you are continuing from episode 1 in the same notebook, data is already loaded. Either way, run the following:

    PYTHON 

    !pip install doubleml     # once per session
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from doubleml.datasets import fetch_401K
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import KFold, cross_val_predict

data = fetch_401K(return_type='DataFrame')
features_base = ['age', 'inc', 'educ', 'fsize', 'marr',
                 'twoearn', 'db', 'pira', 'hown']
X = data[features_base]
y = data['net_tfa']
d = data['e401']

    Step A: predict savings from the confounders

    Our first machine learning model predicts each household’s net financial assets from the nine confounders alone, without being told whether the household was eligible. We use the random forest settings from the DoubleML example (slide 37).

    Each household’s prediction has to come from a model that was not trained on that household. KFold splits the households into three parts, and cross_val_predict trains on two parts and predicts the third, three times over. This is called cross-fitting (slide 33), and we can set it up as follows:

    PYTHON 

    randomForest = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=7, max_features=3, min_samples_leaf=3, random_state=0)
folds = KFold(n_splits=3, shuffle=True, random_state=123)

y_hat = cross_val_predict(randomForest, X, y, cv=folds)
y_resid = y - y_hat

    y_hat is \(\hat{Y}\), the savings we would expect given the confounders, and y_resid is the residual \(Y - \hat{Y}\). In other words, y_resid tells us how much more (or less) a household holds than other households like it.

    Step B: predict eligibility from the confounders

    The second model predicts eligibility from the same confounders. Eligibility is yes or no, so we use a classifier and ask it for the probability of being eligible, which is the second column that method='predict_proba' returns:

    PYTHON 

    randomForest_class = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=5, max_features=4, min_samples_leaf=7, random_state=0)

d_hat = cross_val_predict(randomForest_class, X, d, cv=folds,
                          method='predict_proba')[:, 1]
d_resid = d - d_hat

    d_hat is \(\hat{D}\), the chance that a household like this one is eligible, and d_resid is \(D - \hat{D}\). For an eligible household d_resid is positive, meaning it is more eligible than expected, and for a household that is not eligible it is negative.

    What do the residuals mean for three households?

    Let’s put the predictions and residuals side by side for the first three households:

    PYTHON 

    pd.DataFrame({'net_tfa': y, 'y_hat': y_hat, 'y_resid': y_resid,
              'e401': d, 'd_hat': d_hat, 'd_resid': d_resid}).head(3).round(2)

    OUTPUT 

       net_tfa    y_hat   y_resid  e401  d_hat  d_resid
0      0.0  3356.01 -3356.01     0   0.09   -0.09
1   1015.0  7370.83 -6355.83     0   0.30   -0.30
2  -2000.0   143.99 -2143.99     0   0.39   -0.39

    Take the second household as an example. Given its income, age and so on, the first model expects it to hold about $7,371, but it actually holds $1,015, so its residual savings are about −$6,356. The second model gives a household like this a 30% chance of being eligible. This household is not eligible, so its residual eligibility is 0 − 0.30 = −0.30.

    Step C: one regression

    The final step asks whether households that are more eligible than expected also save more than expected. We answer that with the slope of y_resid on d_resid. With one predictor and no intercept, the least squares slope is the sum of the products divided by the sum of squares, which we can compute directly:

    PYTHON 

    theta_hat = (d_resid @ y_resid) / (d_resid @ d_resid)
print(f"Effect of eligibility, by hand: ${theta_hat:,.0f}")

    OUTPUT 

    Effect of eligibility, by hand: $8,984

    This is close to the $8,910 that DoubleML reports in episode 3. The two are not identical because DoubleML draws its own three folds and its forests make their own random choices. In episode 4 we will see that the choice of model moves the answer by more than this.

    The chart on slide 32 plotted DoubleML’s residuals for all 9,915 households, sorted into 20 groups. We can draw the same chart with our own residuals:

    PYTHON 

    groups = pd.qcut(d_resid, 20, labels=False)
binned = pd.DataFrame({'d_resid': d_resid, 'y_resid': y_resid}).groupby(groups).mean()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 4.5))
ax.axhline(0, color='grey', lw=1)
ax.axvline(0, color='grey', lw=1)
ax.scatter(binned.d_resid, binned.y_resid)
xs = np.array([-1, 1])
ax.plot(xs, theta_hat * xs)
ax.set_xlabel('Residual eligibility (D - D-hat)')
ax.set_ylabel('Residual savings (Y - Y-hat)')
plt.show()

    Each dot is the average for about 500 households with similar residual eligibility. Dots to the left of zero are households that were not eligible, and dots to the right of zero are households that were. The slope of the line is the effect.

    Why the slope of the residuals is the effect

    Slide 32 wrote the final regression as \(Y - \hat{Y} = \theta(D - \hat{D}) + \varepsilon\). This regression comes from the partially linear model, which slide 38 names:

    \[Y = \theta D + g(X) + \varepsilon,\]

    where θ is the effect of eligibility and g(X) is everything the confounders do to savings, whatever its shape. Model 1’s prediction, \(\hat{Y}\), is the average savings of households with the same X, and model 2’s prediction, \(\hat{D}\), is their average eligibility. If we average both sides of the model over households with the same X, ε averages to zero and we get:

    \[\hat{Y} = \theta \hat{D} + g(X).\]

    If we subtract this second equation from the first, g(X) cancels and we are left with:

    \[Y - \hat{Y} = \theta (D - \hat{D}) + \varepsilon.\]

    So regressing residual savings on residual eligibility estimates θ, whatever shape g takes. The machine learning models only have to predict well, and they never have to tell us what g looks like.

    With straight lines, this is ordinary regression

    Steps A to C are older than they look. Frisch and Waugh (1933) showed that if both predictions come from ordinary linear regression, the slope in step C is exactly the coefficient on eligibility from a multiple regression of savings on eligibility and the nine confounders. In other words, when a regression “controls for” X, it is doing these three steps behind the scenes. We can check this by using linear regression for both predictions, fitted on all the data:

    PYTHON 

    import statsmodels.formula.api as smf
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

y_resid_lin = y - LinearRegression().fit(X, y).predict(X)
d_resid_lin = d - LinearRegression().fit(X, d).predict(X)
print(f"Slope of the residuals:     ${(d_resid_lin @ y_resid_lin) / (d_resid_lin @ d_resid_lin):,.2f}")

ols = smf.ols('net_tfa ~ e401 + ' + ' + '.join(features_base), data=data).fit()
print(f"Multiple regression for e401: ${ols.params['e401']:,.2f}")

    OUTPUT 

    Slope of the residuals:     $5,896.20
Multiple regression for e401: $5,896.20

    You should see the same figure on both lines, and this is what “holding the other variables constant” means in a regression. DML keeps this logic and swaps the straight lines for flexible models. The regression’s $5,896 is lower than the forests’ estimate, probably because a straight line in income cannot follow how savings actually rise with income. We will come back to this in episode 4.

    Why do we need cross-fitting?

    Suppose we skip cross-fitting and let a very flexible forest, with no depth limit and leaves of one household, predict the same households it was trained on:

    PYTHON 

    flexible = RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, min_samples_leaf=1, random_state=0)
flexible_class = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, min_samples_leaf=1, random_state=0)

y_resid_in = y - flexible.fit(X, y).predict(X)
d_resid_in = d - flexible_class.fit(X, d).predict_proba(X)[:, 1]
print(f"Residual savings, as a share of the variance of savings: {y_resid_in.var() / y.var():.2f}")
print(f"Effect without cross-fitting: ${(d_resid_in @ y_resid_in) / (d_resid_in @ d_resid_in):,.0f}")

    OUTPUT 

    Residual savings, as a share of the variance of savings: 0.11
Effect without cross-fitting: $9,629

    The forest appears to “explain” almost 90% of the variation in savings. Income and the other confounders cannot really predict savings that well. The forest has partly memorised the households, so their residuals have shrunk towards zero. The estimate is built from those shrunken residuals, and the theory behind DML’s confidence interval no longer applies to it.

    Challenge

    Challenge: the same flexible forests, with cross-fitting

    Repeat the last block, but this time get the predictions with cross_val_predict(..., cv=folds), as we did in steps A and B. What share of the variance of savings is left over now, and what is the estimate? Fill in the blanks below. In this and every later exercise, replace each ____ with your answer before you run the cell: Python reads the blank as a name, so running it unchanged gives NameError: name '____' is not defined.

    PYTHON 

    y_resid_cf = y - cross_val_predict(flexible, X, y, cv=____)
d_resid_cf = d - cross_val_predict(flexible_class, X, d, cv=____, method='predict_proba')[:, 1]
print(f"Residual share: {y_resid_cf.var() / y.var():.2f}")
print(f"Effect with cross-fitting: ${(d_resid_cf @ y_resid_cf) / (d_resid_cf @ d_resid_cf):,.0f}")

    PYTHON 

    y_resid_cf = y - cross_val_predict(flexible, X, y, cv=folds)
d_resid_cf = d - cross_val_predict(flexible_class, X, d, cv=folds, method='predict_proba')[:, 1]
print(f"Residual share: {y_resid_cf.var() / y.var():.2f}")
print(f"Effect with cross-fitting: ${(d_resid_cf @ y_resid_cf) / (d_resid_cf @ d_resid_cf):,.0f}")

    OUTPUT 

    Residual share: 0.84
Effect with cross-fitting: $9,269

    With cross-fitting, 84% of the variation in savings is left over, compared with 11% before. Income and the other confounders predict savings only partly, and the residuals now reflect that. A model cannot memorise a household it never saw, which is why DoubleML always cross-fits.

    The estimate of $9,269 is still a little higher than the $8,984 we got in steps A to C. These unrestricted forests are noisier than the tuned ones from the DoubleML example, and the choice of model moves the answer, which is what episode 4 is about.

    Key Points
    • DML predicts the outcome from the confounders, predicts the treatment from the confounders, and takes the slope of one set of residuals on the other as the effect.
    • A residual is how far a household is from what the confounders predict, in savings or in eligibility, compared with households like it.
    • With straight-line predictions the slope equals the multiple regression coefficient (Frisch and Waugh, 1933), and DML swaps in flexible models for the straight lines.
    • Each prediction must come from a model that did not see that household (cross-fitting), because otherwise flexible models memorise the data and shrink the residuals.

    Content from DML in five steps with DoubleML

    Last updated on 2026-10-30 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How do I run double machine learning on the 401(k) data with DoubleML?
    • How do I read the output from DoubleML?

    Objectives

    • Run the five steps from the slides (load the data, set the roles, choose two models, fit and read the result)
    • Interpret the estimate and its 95% confidence interval
    • Connect DoubleML’s stored predictions to the residuals from episode 2
    Callout

    From the masterclass

    This episode follows the five steps on slides 35 to 39, from “Step 1: load the data” to “Step 5: read the result”. The code for steps 1 to 4 is copied unchanged from slides 35 to 38 (if you came to the workshop, it is the code you ran there), and step 5 reads the output shown on slide 39. If you run the blocks in order, you will get the same numbers as the slides.

    Step 1: load the data

    PYTHON 

    !pip install doubleml     # once per session
import numpy as np
import doubleml as dml
from doubleml.datasets import fetch_401K

data = fetch_401K(return_type='DataFrame')
print(data[['e401', 'net_tfa']]
      .groupby('e401').mean().diff())

    OUTPUT 

              net_tfa
e401
0             NaN
1     19559.34475

    You should see the same raw gap as in episode 1, with eligible households holding $19,559 more on average.

    Step 2: tell DoubleML which variable is which

    There is no machine learning in this step, yet it matters more than any of the others. We give DoubleML the outcome in y_col, the treatment in d_cols and the confounders in x_cols, and we chose those confounders from the causal diagram in episode 1.

    PYTHON 

    features_base = ['age', 'inc', 'educ',
                 'fsize', 'marr', 'twoearn',
                 'db', 'pira', 'hown']

data_dml_base = dml.DoubleMLData(data,
    y_col='net_tfa',         # outcome
    d_cols='e401',           # treatment
    x_cols=features_base)    # confounders

    Let’s print the object to check what DoubleML will use:

    PYTHON 

    print(data_dml_base)

    OUTPUT 

    ================== DoubleMLData Object ==================

------------------ Data summary      ------------------
Outcome variable: net_tfa
Treatment variable(s): ['e401']
Covariates: ['age', 'inc', 'educ', 'fsize', 'marr', 'twoearn', 'db', 'pira', 'hown']
Instrument variable(s): None
No. Observations: 9915
------------------ DataFrame info    ------------------
<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 9915 entries, 0 to 9914
Columns: 14 entries, nifa to hown
dtypes: float32(4), int8(10)
memory usage: 251.9 KB

    Step 3: choose the two machine learning models

    We need two random forests. The first, randomForest, predicts savings (Y) from X and is model 1 in the diagram on slide 30. The second, randomForest_class, predicts eligibility (D) from X and is model 2. Eligibility is a yes or no variable, so model 2 has to be a classifier. We use the settings from DoubleML’s own example, which set the number of trees at 500 and limit how deep each tree may grow, how many variables each split considers and how few households a leaf may hold.

    PYTHON 

    from sklearn.ensemble import (
    RandomForestRegressor,
    RandomForestClassifier)

randomForest = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=7,
    max_features=3, min_samples_leaf=3)

randomForest_class = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=5,
    max_features=4, min_samples_leaf=7)

    Step 4: fit the model

    PYTHON 

    np.random.seed(123)  # same result each run
dml_plr_forest = dml.DoubleMLPLR(
    data_dml_base,
    ml_l = randomForest,
    ml_m = randomForest_class,
    n_folds = 3)

dml_plr_forest.fit(store_predictions=True)

forest_summary = dml_plr_forest.summary
print(forest_summary.round(2))

    OUTPUT 

             coef  std err     t  P>|t|    2.5 %    97.5 %
e401  8909.63  1321.82  6.74    0.0  6318.91  11500.36

    DoubleMLPLR is the partially linear regression model named on slide 38, Y = θD + g(X) + ε. In other words, eligibility has a single effect θ on savings, while the confounders can affect savings through a function g of any shape. (Episode 2 showed why the slope of the residuals estimates θ.) Setting n_folds = 3 asks for three-fold cross-fitting. When we call fit(), DoubleML runs everything we did in episode 2. It trains both forests on two folds and predicts the third, rotates the folds, and then regresses residual savings on residual eligibility.

    Notice that we set the seed just before creating the model. DoubleML draws the random split into folds when the model is created, and the forests make their own random choices when they are fitted. Setting the seed before both steps fixes all of these choices, so you get the same numbers as on the slides. Without the seed the estimate changes from run to run, and in episode 5 we repeat the split five times and get anything from $8,821 to $9,169. The numbers may also differ slightly if you have a different version of scikit-learn or DoubleML.

    Step 5: read the result

    Each column of the summary tells us something different:

    • coef is the estimated effect of eligibility on net financial assets, about $8,910.
    • std err is its standard error, about $1,322.
    • t and P>|t| test the hypothesis of no effect. The 0.0 is rounding, and p is below .001.
    • 2.5 % and 97.5 % are the two ends of the 95% confidence interval, which runs from $6,319 to $11,500.

    Compare this with the raw gap of $19,559. Once we take the nine confounders out of both savings and eligibility, the estimate drops to less than half of the raw gap, so about 54% of the gap was confounding. The income bands in episode 1 suggest that much of it comes through income. The estimate still assumes that there is no confounder outside X, and this is the assumption to argue about. We will come back to it in episode 5.

    The residuals DoubleML used

    Because we fitted the model with store_predictions=True, DoubleML kept its cross-fitted predictions. This means we can redo step C from episode 2 with DoubleML’s own residuals:

    PYTHON 

    y_resid = data['net_tfa'] - dml_plr_forest.predictions['ml_l'][:, 0, 0]
d_resid = data['e401'] - dml_plr_forest.predictions['ml_m'][:, 0, 0]
print(f"Slope of the residuals: ${(d_resid @ y_resid) / (d_resid @ d_resid):,.2f}")
print(f"DoubleML's estimate:    ${dml_plr_forest.coef[0]:,.2f}")

    OUTPUT 

    Slope of the residuals: $8,909.63
DoubleML's estimate:    $8,909.63

    You should see that the two numbers match to the cent. These are the same residuals plotted on slide 32. The [:, 0, 0] is there because predictions['ml_l'] has three dimensions (households, repetitions of the split and treatments), and we have only one repetition and one treatment.

    Challenge

    Challenge: five folds instead of three

    Refit the model with n_folds = 5 and keep the seed as it is. How much does the estimate move, and is the change large compared with the standard error? Replace the ____ with the number of folds before you run the cell:

    PYTHON 

    np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_forest5 = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base, ml_l = randomForest,
                                  ml_m = randomForest_class, n_folds = ____)
dml_plr_forest5.fit()
print(dml_plr_forest5.summary.round(2))

    PYTHON 

    np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_forest5 = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base, ml_l = randomForest,
                                  ml_m = randomForest_class, n_folds = 5)
dml_plr_forest5.fit()
print(dml_plr_forest5.summary.round(2))

    OUTPUT 

             coef  std err     t  P>|t|    2.5 %    97.5 %
e401  8915.54  1305.55  6.83    0.0  6356.71  11474.37

    The estimate barely moves, from $8,910 to $8,916, which is a tiny fraction of the standard error. With five folds each model trains on 80% of the households instead of two thirds. Both choices are reasonable, so pick one before you look at the answer and report which one you used.

    Key Points
    • DoubleMLData sets the roles of the variables, DoubleMLPLR combines the data with two learners, and fit() runs the cross-fitting and the final regression.
    • With random forests and three folds, we estimate that 401(k) eligibility raised net financial assets by about $8,910 (95% CI $6,319 to $11,500), against a raw gap of $19,559.
    • Setting np.random.seed() just before creating the model keeps the folds and forests the same on every run.
    • DoubleML’s estimate is exactly the slope of its stored residuals.

    Content from Same question, four learners

    Last updated on 2026-10-30 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • Does the answer depend on which machine learning model we use?
    • Why does lasso need help from squared terms?

    Objectives

    • Fit the partially linear model with lasso, a random forest, a decision tree and boosting
    • Explain why lasso with the raw variables gives a lower estimate than lasso with squared terms
    • Summarise the four estimates in a table and a chart, and decide how to report them
    Callout

    From the masterclass

    Slide 40, “You can then repeat the DML process, but change the ML method”, showed the chart you will make at the end of this episode. It also suggested reporting the spread across learners as a form of sensitivity analysis. In this episode we fit each learner in turn and see why lasso needs extra terms, following the DoubleML example cell by cell.

    Set up

    We start with the imports from the DoubleML example, followed by the data and the data object from episode 3. We have added three lines of our own. The first installs DoubleML if it is not there already, for example in a fresh Colab notebook. The warnings filter hides notices from scikit-learn saying that the lasso classifier’s penalty argument will change in a future version (with the versions pinned for this lesson it works as it should). The display.width line stops pandas from hiding columns of the summaries.

    PYTHON 

    !pip install doubleml     # once per session
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings('ignore', category=FutureWarning)  # scikit-learn notices about future versions

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import doubleml as dml
from doubleml.datasets import fetch_401K

from sklearn.preprocessing import PolynomialFeatures
from sklearn.linear_model import LassoCV, LogisticRegressionCV
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier, RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, DecisionTreeRegressor
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

from xgboost import XGBClassifier, XGBRegressor

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
import seaborn as sns

pd.set_option('display.width', 120)
data = fetch_401K(return_type='DataFrame')

# Set up basic model: Specify variables for data-backend
features_base = ['age', 'inc', 'educ', 'fsize', 'marr',
                 'twoearn', 'db', 'pira', 'hown']

# Initialize DoubleMLData (data-backend of DoubleML)
data_dml_base = dml.DoubleMLData(data,
                                 y_col='net_tfa',
                                 d_cols='e401',
                                 x_cols=features_base)

    If from xgboost import ... fails on a Mac with a message about libomp, have a look at the Setup page.

    Lasso

    Lasso is a linear regression that shrinks small coefficients towards zero and drops some variables altogether. We need two lasso models, LassoCV for savings and a penalised logistic regression for eligibility. Both choose how hard to shrink by five-fold cross-validation, and both need the variables on the same scale, which is why each pipeline starts with StandardScaler:

    PYTHON 

    # Initialize learners
Cs = 0.0001*np.logspace(0, 4, 10)
lasso = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LassoCV(cv=5, max_iter=10000))
lasso_class = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(),
                            LogisticRegressionCV(cv=5, penalty='l1', solver='liblinear',
                                                 Cs = Cs, max_iter=1000))

np.random.seed(123)
# Initialize DoubleMLPLR model
dml_plr_lasso = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base,
                                ml_l = lasso,
                                ml_m = lasso_class,
                                n_folds = 3)

dml_plr_lasso.fit(store_predictions=True)
print(dml_plr_lasso.summary)

    OUTPUT 

                 coef      std err         t     P>|t|        2.5 %       97.5 %
e401  5722.474647  1380.619171  4.144861  0.000034  3016.510795  8428.438499

    Lasso gives about $5,722, well below the $8,910 we got from the random forest in episode 3. Lasso fits straight lines, so it treats each extra $1,000 of income as adding the same amount to savings at every income level. Savings rise faster than that at higher incomes, and whatever the straight line misses stays in the residuals as confounding.

    The DoubleML example deals with this by giving lasso squared terms for the four continuous confounders, so that it can draw curves. The code below builds a flexible data object with age, age², income, income² and so on:

    PYTHON 

    # Set up a model according to regression formula with polynomials
features = data.copy()[['marr', 'twoearn', 'db', 'pira', 'hown']]

poly_dict = {'age': 2,
             'inc': 2,
             'educ': 2,
             'fsize': 2}
for key, degree in poly_dict.items():
    poly = PolynomialFeatures(degree, include_bias=False)
    data_transf = poly.fit_transform(data[[key]])
    x_cols = poly.get_feature_names_out([key])
    data_transf = pd.DataFrame(data_transf, columns=x_cols)
    
    features = pd.concat((features, data_transf),
                          axis=1, sort=False)
model_data = pd.concat((data.copy()[['net_tfa', 'e401']], features.copy()),
                        axis=1, sort=False)

# Initialize DoubleMLData (data-backend of DoubleML)
data_dml_flex = dml.DoubleMLData(model_data, y_col='net_tfa', d_cols='e401')

    PYTHON 

    print(data_dml_flex)

    OUTPUT 

    ================== DoubleMLData Object ==================

------------------ Data summary      ------------------
Outcome variable: net_tfa
Treatment variable(s): ['e401']
Covariates: ['marr', 'twoearn', 'db', 'pira', 'hown', 'age', 'age^2', 'inc', 'inc^2', 'educ', 'educ^2', 'fsize', 'fsize^2']
Instrument variable(s): None
No. Observations: 9915
------------------ DataFrame info    ------------------
<class 'pandas.DataFrame'>
RangeIndex: 9915 entries, 0 to 9914
Columns: 15 entries, net_tfa to fsize^2
dtypes: float32(3), float64(6), int8(6)
memory usage: 639.2 KB

    Now we can fit lasso again, this time on the flexible data:

    PYTHON 

    # Estimate the ATE in the flexible model with lasso

np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_lasso = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_flex,
                                ml_l = lasso,
                                ml_m = lasso_class,
                                n_folds = 3)

dml_plr_lasso.fit(store_predictions=True)
lasso_summary = dml_plr_lasso.summary

print(lasso_summary)

    OUTPUT 

                 coef      std err         t         P>|t|        2.5 %        97.5 %
e401  8974.791097  1324.323636  6.776887  1.227932e-11  6379.164467  11570.417727

    With the squared terms, lasso gives about $8,975, which is close to the random forest. Lasso can only work with the variables we hand it, while random forests and boosting find curves without being told.

    Random forest

    These are steps 3 and 4 from episode 3, laid out as in the DoubleML example:

    PYTHON 

    # Random Forest
randomForest = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=7, max_features=3, min_samples_leaf=3)
randomForest_class = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=5, max_features=4, min_samples_leaf=7)

np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_forest = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base,
                                 ml_l = randomForest,
                                 ml_m = randomForest_class,
                                 n_folds = 3)
dml_plr_forest.fit(store_predictions=True)
forest_summary = dml_plr_forest.summary

print(forest_summary)

    OUTPUT 

                 coef      std err         t         P>|t|        2.5 %        97.5 %
e401  8909.634078  1321.822289  6.740417  1.579322e-11  6318.909997  11500.358158

    You should get the same $8,910 as in episode 3.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: a single decision tree

    Fit the model with one decision tree for each prediction, using the settings from the example. The ccp_alpha argument prunes the tree, while min_samples_split and min_samples_leaf stop it splitting small groups. Fill in the two learners by replacing each ____ with one of the two models (one predicts savings, the other eligibility) before you run the cell:

    PYTHON

trees = DecisionTreeRegressor(
    max_depth=30, ccp_alpha=0.0047, min_samples_split=203, min_samples_leaf=67)
trees_class = DecisionTreeClassifier(

                               ml_l = ____,

tree_summary = dml_plr_tree.summary

print(tree_summary)

    max_depth=30, ccp_alpha=0.0047, min_samples_split=203, min_samples_leaf=67)

    max_depth=30, ccp_alpha=0.0042, min_samples_split=104, min_samples_leaf=34)

np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_tree = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base,
                               ml_l = trees,

tree_summary = dml_plr_tree.summary

    OUTPUT 

                coef      std err         t         P>|t|        2.5 %        97.5 %
e401  8260.06428  1348.624798  6.124805  9.079458e-10  5616.808246  10903.320314

    A single tree gives about $8,260. Its predictions move in a few dozen steps, so its residuals keep a little more of the confounding than the forest’s do, though the estimate still lands in the same range.

    Challenge

    Challenge 2: boosting

    Now try boosted trees from the XGBoost library. As slide 26 showed, boosting grows trees in sequence, with each tree fixing the mistakes of the one before. Here eta is the learning rate and n_estimators is the number of trees. Fill in the two learners by replacing each ____ with one of the two models before you run the cell:

    PYTHON 

    # Boosted Trees
boost = XGBRegressor(n_jobs=1, objective = "reg:squarederror",
                     eta=0.1, n_estimators=35)

                            objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
                            eta=0.1, n_estimators=34)

np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_boost = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base,
                                ml_l = ____,
                                ml_m = ____,
                                n_folds = 3)
dml_plr_boost.fit(store_predictions=True)
boost_summary = dml_plr_boost.summary

print(boost_summary)

                            objective = "binary:logistic", eval_metric = "logloss",
                            eta=0.1, n_estimators=34)

np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_boost = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base,
                                ml_l = boost,
                                ml_m = boost_class,
                                n_folds = 3)
dml_plr_boost.fit(store_predictions=True)
boost_summary = dml_plr_boost.summary

print(boost_summary)

    OUTPUT 

                 coef      std err         t         P>|t|        2.5 %        97.5 %
e401  8336.661463  1391.026647  5.993172  2.057874e-09  5610.299334  11063.023593

    Boosting gives about $8,337. Recent versions of XGBoost may print a warning that use_label_encoder is not used. The argument is left over from older versions and does no harm, so you can ignore the warning.

    Putting the four together

    Let’s collect the four summaries into one table. This uses tree_summary and boost_summary from the two challenges, so if you skipped them, run their solutions first:

    PYTHON 

    plr_summary = pd.concat((lasso_summary, forest_summary, tree_summary, boost_summary))
plr_summary.index = ['lasso', 'forest', 'tree', 'xgboost']
print(plr_summary[['coef', '2.5 %', '97.5 %']])

    OUTPUT 

                    coef        2.5 %        97.5 %
lasso    8974.791097  6379.164467  11570.417727
forest   8909.634078  6318.909997  11500.358158
tree     8260.064280  5616.808246  10903.320314
xgboost  8336.661463  5610.299334  11063.023593

    We can show the same numbers as a chart with error bars:

    PYTHON 

    errors = np.full((2, plr_summary.shape[0]), np.nan)
errors[0, :] = plr_summary['coef'] - plr_summary['2.5 %']
errors[1, :] = plr_summary['97.5 %'] - plr_summary['coef']
plt.errorbar(plr_summary.index, plr_summary.coef, fmt='o', yerr=errors)
plt.ylim([0, 12500])

plt.title('Partially Linear Regression Model (PLR)')
plt.xlabel('ML method')
_ =  plt.ylabel('Coefficients and 95%-CI')
plt.show()

    Each dot in the chart is one estimate of the effect of eligibility, and each line is its 95% confidence interval. You should see that the four estimates lie between about $8,260 and $8,975, and that their intervals overlap almost entirely.

    Discussion

    Which number would you report?

    The four estimates differ by about $700, which is around half a standard error. Good practice is to choose the main specification before you see the results, report it, and show the others alongside it, as the DoubleML example does. If you pick the number you like best after the fact, the robustness check turns into a search for significance.

    Keep the lasso with raw variables ($5,722) in mind as well. A learner that cannot follow the shape of the confounders leaves confounding behind, and nothing in the output will warn you about it.

    Key Points
    • DoubleML accepts any scikit-learn-style model for the two predictions, ml_l for the outcome and ml_m for the treatment.
    • On the 401(k) data, lasso with squared terms, a random forest, a decision tree and boosting give estimates from $8,260 to $8,975.
    • Lasso with only the raw variables gives $5,722, probably because its straight lines miss the curve in income and the confounding they miss stays in the estimate.
    • It is good practice to choose the main estimate in advance and report the other learners’ estimates alongside it.

    Content from Checks, and your own research

    Last updated on 2026-10-30 | Edit this page

    Overview

    Questions

    • How strong would an unmeasured confounder need to be to change the answer?
    • How much does the estimate depend on the random split into folds?
    • Where could DML help in my own research?

    Objectives

    • Run and interpret DoubleML’s sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding
    • Repeat the cross-fitting with several random splits and report the spread
    • Identify a question from your own research where DML could help

    Set up

    Let’s start by fitting the random forest model from episode 3 again, written a little more compactly this time:

    PYTHON 

    !pip install doubleml     # once per session
import numpy as np
import doubleml as dml
from doubleml.datasets import fetch_401K
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor, RandomForestClassifier

data = fetch_401K(return_type='DataFrame')
features_base = ['age', 'inc', 'educ', 'fsize', 'marr',
                 'twoearn', 'db', 'pira', 'hown']
data_dml_base = dml.DoubleMLData(data, y_col='net_tfa', d_cols='e401', x_cols=features_base)

randomForest = RandomForestRegressor(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=7, max_features=3, min_samples_leaf=3)
randomForest_class = RandomForestClassifier(
    n_estimators=500, max_depth=5, max_features=4, min_samples_leaf=7)

np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_forest = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base, ml_l = randomForest,
                                 ml_m = randomForest_class, n_folds = 3)
dml_plr_forest.fit(store_predictions=True)
print(dml_plr_forest.summary.round(2))

    OUTPUT 

             coef  std err     t  P>|t|    2.5 %    97.5 %
e401  8909.63  1321.82  6.74    0.0  6318.91  11500.36

    How strong would an unmeasured confounder need to be?

    Every estimate so far rests on the assumption that the nine confounders (income, age, education, family size, marital status, two earners, a defined benefit pension, IRA participation and home ownership) capture everything that drives both eligibility and savings. In episode 1 we named the obvious worry, which is a preference for saving. We have no measure of it in the data, so instead we ask how strong it would have to be to change our answer.

    DoubleML’s sensitivity analysis (Chernozhukov et al., 2026) describes this hypothetical confounder with two numbers:

    • cf_y is the share of the residual variation in savings that the confounder would explain.
    • cf_d is how much the confounder would add to the explained variation in eligibility.

    Let’s try a confounder that explains 4% of the residual variation in savings and adds 3% for eligibility:

    PYTHON 

    dml_plr_forest.sensitivity_analysis(cf_y=0.04, cf_d=0.03)
print(dml_plr_forest.sensitivity_summary)

    OUTPUT 

    ================== Sensitivity Analysis ==================

------------------ Scenario          ------------------
Significance Level: level=0.95
Sensitivity parameters: cf_y=0.04; cf_d=0.03, rho=1.0

------------------ Bounds with CI    ------------------
         CI lower  theta lower        theta   theta upper      CI upper
e401  2359.496777  4610.983759  8909.634078  13208.284397  15430.415812

------------------ Robustness Values ------------------
      H_0    RV (%)   RVa (%)
e401  0.0  7.029209  5.233154

    The theta lower and theta upper columns show how far the estimate could move if a confounder that strong existed, and you should see that the whole interval still lies well above zero. CI lower and CI upper widen those bounds a little further to allow for sampling error.

    The last block of the output gives the robustness value, RV. This is the strength a confounder would need, with the same share for both cf_y and cf_d, to push the estimate all the way to zero. RVa is the same idea with sampling error allowed for.

    Whether a confounder that strong is plausible is a judgement about the setting, and the data cannot make that judgement for you. What the analysis does is turn a vague “there might be confounding” into a number that you and a reviewer can argue about.

    Challenge

    Challenge 1: a stronger confounder

    Rerun the sensitivity analysis with cf_y=0.08, cf_d=0.08. Does the lower bound for the estimate stay above zero?

    PYTHON 

    dml_plr_forest.sensitivity_analysis(cf_y=0.08, cf_d=0.08)
print(dml_plr_forest.sensitivity_summary)

    OUTPUT 

    ================== Sensitivity Analysis ==================

------------------ Scenario          ------------------
Significance Level: level=0.95
Sensitivity parameters: cf_y=0.08; cf_d=0.08, rho=1.0

------------------ Bounds with CI    ------------------
         CI lower  theta lower        theta  theta upper      CI upper
e401 -3820.980088 -1283.868465  8909.634078  19103.13662  21578.115315

------------------ Robustness Values ------------------
      H_0    RV (%)   RVa (%)
e401  0.0  7.029209  5.233154

    A confounder this strong is above the robustness value, so the lower bound drops below zero. In other words, if such a confounder existed, we could no longer rule out an effect of zero. The robustness value would have told you this already, without trying values one by one.

    How much does the split into folds matter?

    The three folds are drawn at random, so it is fair to ask how much our estimate depends on that one draw. Setting n_rep=5 repeats the whole cross-fitting with five different random splits and reports the median estimate. Expect this to take about five times as long as a single fit:

    PYTHON 

    np.random.seed(123)
dml_plr_forest_rep = dml.DoubleMLPLR(data_dml_base, ml_l = randomForest,
                                     ml_m = randomForest_class, n_folds = 3, n_rep = 5)
dml_plr_forest_rep.fit()
print("Estimate from each split:", dml_plr_forest_rep.all_coef.round(0).ravel().tolist())
print(dml_plr_forest_rep.summary.round(2))

    OUTPUT 

    Estimate from each split: [8947.0, 9012.0, 9099.0, 9169.0, 8821.0]
        coef  std err     t  P>|t|   2.5 %    97.5 %
e401  9012.1  1317.42  6.84    0.0  6430.0  11594.21

    The first line lists the five estimates, each from the same model on a different random split. Their spread is small compared with the standard error of about $1,300, so the choice of split is not what drives the result here. With small samples or very flexible learners the spread can be much larger, so it is good practice to repeat the split for any result you report.

    A checklist for before you run DML

    The table below gathers the steps from this lesson that you would work through for a question of your own. Most of them are decisions about research design and need little or no code. The right-hand column shows where each step came up.

    Step In this lesson
    Write the causal question: treatment, outcome, population Episode 1
    Draw a causal diagram (DAG) and pick the confounders from it Episode 1
    Leave out mediators and colliders (bad controls) Episode 1, challenge 1
    Explain why no major confounder is missing Episode 1, challenge 2
    Check overlap between treated and untreated Not covered here; see DoubleML’s 401(k) example
    Try several ML models and data splits, and report the spread Episodes 4 and 5
    Run a sensitivity analysis for unmeasured confounding Episode 5
    Report a simple regression alongside, for comparison Episode 2
    Discussion

    Discussion: where could DML help in your own research?

    DML suits questions that ask what would happen if something changed, where an experiment is not possible but you have data on the things that drive both the treatment and the outcome. The masterclass gave three examples from different fields (slide 5): would a follow-up phone call reduce hospital readmissions, would offering a workplace pension raise savings, and would tutoring help pupils pass? Think of a question like these from your own work, and consider:

    • What is the treatment, and what is the outcome?
    • What affects both of them, and do your data measure it?
    • Which confounder could you not measure, and would it make the estimate too high or too low?
    • Would DML add anything over a regression with controls? It helps most when there are many confounders, or when their effects are unlikely to be straight lines.

    If you are working through the lesson with others, compare your answers. Questions from quite different fields often turn out to have the same structure.

    Where to go next

    If you want to take DML further, these are good places to start:

    • The DoubleML example that this lesson follows, in both Python and R.
    • The DoubleML documentation, which covers other designs, including DML for difference-in-differences (DoubleMLDID). Part 2 of the slides introduced DID.
    • Chernozhukov et al. (2024), Applied causal inference powered by ML and AI, which is free online with notebooks.
    • Hünermund et al. (2023), on why handing DML every available variable can make estimates worse.
    • The Reference page, which has a glossary and the full reference list.
    Key Points
    • A sensitivity analysis asks how strong an unmeasured confounder would need to be to change the conclusion, and the robustness value summarises the answer in one number.
    • Repeating the cross-fitting with several random splits (n_rep) shows how much the estimate depends on the split.
    • DML suits questions about what would happen if something changed, when an experiment is not possible but the confounders are measured.
    • Most of the work in a credible DML analysis goes into design, which covers the question, the causal diagram, the confounders, overlap and the sensitivity of the result.
